# Peripherals and SoC Integration

## Concepts

A peripheral includes more than its datapath. It also needs software-visible state, reset behavior, clock assumptions, and handling of inputs that originate outside the clock domain.

UART reception bridges a timed serial waveform and a parallel byte interface. Synchronizing the asynchronous input reduces metastability risk, while the receiver state machine samples serial bits. An internal ready/valid connection can stall a byte transfer, but it cannot force an external UART sender to stop transmitting.

## Implementation

The `uart_loopback` example connects `uart_rx` to `uart_tx` through a byte-wide ready/valid channel. The wrapper defaults to a 50 MHz clock and 115200 baud; its reset is synchronous and active high. The receiver contains a two-register input synchronizer.

The loopback has no memory-mapped interface and is not a complete SoC UART peripheral. For processor integration, add receive/transmit buffering, status registers, an overrun policy, and interrupt conditions. Document the clock-to-baud divider and its rounding error. Inspect buffering and overflow behavior rather than assuming backpressure protects the incoming serial stream.

The UART RX/TX implementation discussed here carries Apache-2.0 license headers attributed to Two Sigma Open Source, LLC. Preserve these notices and license requirements when distributing those files.

## Hands-on Experiments

Simulate a single serial frame, consecutive frames, and delayed transmitter readiness. Vary the sender's bit period around the nominal value and record the tested range. Check reset during a frame and specify the expected loss or recovery behavior.

Draw a domain-crossing table for serial input, system clock, and reset. Extend the loopback into a memory-mapped peripheral and verify software access independently from serial timing.
